findings.title: Async legacy writes use the request context, which is canceled when the handler returns
findings.body: Mode 3 launches the legacy write in a goroutine using the incoming request context: `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. In Go's HTTP server, the request context is canceled as soon as the handler returns, and these methods return the unified-storage result immediately after starting the goroutine. The legacy `Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection` calls (also at lines 110, 135 and 163) therefore commonly run with an already-canceled context, so the shadow write to legacy fails and the safety copy is never made. Derive the goroutine context from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (preserving request values) or a fresh context with an explicit timeout.

findings.title: Fire-and-forget legacy writes can be applied out of order
findings.body: All mode 3 legacy writes are independent goroutines with no per-object serialization. Two sequential updates to the same object can complete their legacy writes in reverse order, leaving legacy with the older state; a delete followed by a re-create can likewise leave the shadow store missing or containing an object after the unified store already reflects the opposite operation. Because the legacy write is meant as a safety copy, this silently makes the two stores diverge. A per-key queue/worker or version/order check is needed if legacy is expected to remain consistent.

findings.title: Mode 3 records several operations under the wrong metric or label
findings.body: The metrics in this file are mis-attributed. A unified-storage create failure is recorded with `recordLegacyDuration` (line 45), and a unified-storage update failure is also recorded with `recordLegacyDuration` (line 129), even though no legacy call has happened. Delete success passes the object `name` as the `kind` argument to `recordStorageDuration` (line 106), which both mislabels the series and creates unbounded `kind` label cardinality. DeleteCollection's async legacy call records `recordStorageDuration` instead of `recordLegacyDuration` (line 166). These produce incorrect dashboards/alerts and misleading legacy vs. storage latency/error rates.

findings.title: Legacy write failures in async mode are never logged
findings.body: Every async goroutine discards the legacy error and only calls a metrics recording function, e.g. `_, errObjectSt := d.Legacy.Create(...)` followed by `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`. There is no `log.Error`, unlike the previous synchronous implementation. Since these writes are fire-and-forget, operators have no log evidence when the shadow write fails, making the safety mechanism effectively undiagnosable. Log the error (including object identity and method) in each async legacy path.

findings.title: Create error test configures the wrong store and will hit an unexpected mock call
findings.body: The case named "error when creating object in the unified store fails" sets `setupLegacyFn` to return an error and never sets a `Storage.Create` expectation. Mode 3's `Create` calls `Storage.Create` first, so this test invokes the storage mock without an expectation and fails with a testify panic rather than exercising a unified-storage failure. Configure `setupStorageFn` for the error and, if the legacy path is to be covered, set the legacy expectation separately.

findings.title: Delete/DeleteCollection success tests do not account for the async legacy mock call
findings.body: The success cases for `TestMode3_Delete` and `TestMode3_DeleteCollection` only set up the Storage mock. Mode 3 always launches a goroutine that calls `Legacy.Delete`/`Legacy.DeleteCollection`, but there is no legacy expectation and the tests do not wait for the goroutine. With testify's bare `mock.Mock`, the unexpected call panics; even if it did not, the test returns before the legacy write happens and never asserts that the shadow delete occurred. Add legacy expectations and a synchronization mechanism (or refactor to inject a synchronous executor) to verify the async write.

findings.title: Mode 3 integration subtests read legacy before the async shadow write can complete
findings.body: The new mode 3 subtests reuse `doPlaylistTests`, which assumes writes made through the k8s API are immediately visible through the legacy `/api/playlists` API (for example the list comparison around lines 516-531 and `getFromBothAPIs` after k8s create/update/delete). Mode 3 writes to legacy asynchronously, so the legacy read can race ahead of the shadow write and see stale or missing data. These mode 3 subtests will be flaky/failing even if the implementation is correct; they need to poll/wait for legacy convergence or use a synchronous test mode for immediate-visibility assertions.
